items.text: Note the layout: 8 columns, 124 data rows under the header. Run COUNTA on OrderID and look for odd values.

items.title: Clean
items.text: Remove the 5 blank rows, then keep each OrderID once, then standardise Region. Log each count.

items.title: Add the helper column
items.text: Revenue in column I: `=F2*G2`, filled down to the last order.

items.title: Answer the questions
items.text: With formulas first, then confirm each with a PivotTable.

items.title: Chart and write
items.text: One honest chart, then a short report with the answer first and the caveats stated.

blocks.text: Your checkpoints
These numbers should come out the same for anyone who follows the cleaning rules, which is why they make good checkpoints. If one of yours differs, stop and find out why before going on.

blocks.caption: Checkpoint log for the practice file

blocks.text: If your total is R9,152, you added the repeated orders. If a region total looks low, check for trailing spaces in Region. If a region appears several times in a PivotTable, the standardising step is incomplete.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.text: Backup, then blanks, then duplicates, then text, then calculations. Each step removes a problem that would confuse the next one.

blocks.title: What a stubborn mismatch looks like
blocks.text: A learner's Johannesburg total shows R2,498 instead of R2,712 after removing duplicates. Everything else seems fine. The cause is the stray spaces: some Johannesburg rows have a space before or after the name, and the SUMIF skips them. TRIM, then recalculate.
Finish with a chart and a finding

Make a column chart of revenue by region, with the axis starting at zero and a title that states the finding: "Johannesburg leads Cape Town by only R133 across three months". Then write the first lines of your report, answer first. You have done the full job.

blocks.title: Run the whole routine
blocks.intro: Use the café practice file. Allow 60 to 90 minutes, and keep your log open.
tasks: Back up the raw data, clean it, and confirm each checkpoint in the table.
Add the Revenue column and calculate total revenue and the average order value.
Build a region PivotTable, make a chart, and write a four-line report with a caveat.
blocks.reflection: Which step took longest, and what would you automate if you had to repeat this every month?

blocks.prompt: You remove blank rows and duplicates from the practice file and calculate total revenue. You get R9,152. What most likely happened?
options: The repeated orders were still in the data
The blank rows were counted twice
Region spellings were not standardised
The Revenue column was formatted as currency
blocks.explain: R9,152 is the total of all 119 non-blank rows, including the nine repeated orders. The correct cleaned total is R8,542.

lessons.title: Eight question types, worked on the practice file

blocks.text: The final practical asks eight questions of a fresh dataset with the same layout as the café file. Here are the eight question types, each worked on the practice file, so you know what a careful answer looks like. These answers belong to the practice file only. Your practical uses different data, so its answers will differ.

blocks.caption: The eight questions on the practice file (110 clean orders)
rows: Orders after removing blank rows and duplicate OrderIDs
Orders in a given month for a given category
A category's share of total revenue

blocks.text: How each one is found

blocks.label: Formulas used (clean data in rows 2 to 111, Revenue in I)
blocks.text:
1  =COUNTA(A2:A111)
2  =SUM(I2:I111)
3  PivotTable: Region in rows, Sum of Revenue in values, sorted
4  =SUMIF(C2:C111,"Johannesburg",I2:I111)
5  =AVERAGE(I2:I111)   or   =SUM(I2:I111)/COUNTA(A2:A111)
6  PivotTable: Product in rows, Sum of Quantity, sorted
7  =COUNTIFS(E2:E111,"Coffee",B2:B111,">="&DATE(2026,2,1),B2:B111,"<"&DATE(2026,3,1))
8  =SUMIF(E2:E111,"Bakery",I2:I111)/SUM(I2:I111)
Question 5 uses the full average, 77.6545..., shown as R77.65. Question 8 returns 0.1566, which is 15.7% when shown to one decimal place. Round at the end only, never in the middle of a calculation.
Two traps worth seeing

Best-selling by units is not the same as best-selling by revenue. Cappuccino leads on both here, with 55 units and R1,980. But second place differs: Rooibos latte is next by units with 23, while Chicken wrap is next by revenue with R884. Read the question: "best-selling" in the practical is measured in units.

For question 7, the month and the category both matter. Coffee orders in February number 12. Coffee orders in March number 21. Tea orders in February number 10. Filtering on only one of the two conditions would give a different, wrong figure.

blocks.title: Orders are not units
blocks.text: Counting rows counts orders. Summing Quantity counts units. A single order of 5 soups is one order and five units.

blocks.title: Show the denominator
blocks.text: For a share, say what it is a share of. Bakery is 15.7% of total revenue. It is not 15.7% of orders; by orders it is a different number.

blocks.title: Answer all eight on the practice file
blocks.intro: Use your cleaned file and write each answer next to its question number.
tasks: Find all eight answers and compare them with the table above.
For any answer that differs, find the cause before correcting anything.
Then answer two new questions of your own: Tea orders in March and the revenue share of Coffee. Check the second against the shares given in this course.
blocks.reflection: Which question type needed the most care, and what mistake would it have been easy to make?

blocks.prompt: On the practice file, you count 12 orders for the category Coffee. Which month and category pair does this answer?
options: Coffee in February
Coffee in March
Tea in February
Bakery in March
blocks.explain: The cross-tab gives Coffee as 11 in January, 12 in February and 21 in March. Tea in February was 10 and Bakery in March was 8.

lessons.title: The final practical: how to do it carefully

blocks.text: In the final practical you download a fresh dataset with the same shape as the café file: the same eight columns and different orders, so expect similar untidiness and check for it. You answer eight questions about it, and you need six correct to pass. Nothing in it is a trick, but small slips are easy to make and each one shifts a number.

The eight questions are the types you just practised: orders left after cleaning, total revenue, the top region and its revenue, average order value, best-selling product by units, orders in one month for one category, and a category's percentage share of revenue. You already know how to find each.
A careful routine

items.title: Download and back up
items.text: Save the file, keep an untouched Raw sheet and work on a copy.

items.title: Clean in the right order
items.text: Remove blank rows, keep each OrderID once, then fix the Region spellings. Log every count.

items.title: Add Revenue
items.text: Quantity times UnitPrice in a helper column, filled down to the last order.

items.title: Answer with formulas
items.text: Use SUM, COUNTIFS, SUMIF and a PivotTable where it helps.

items.title: Check each answer a second way
items.text: Confirm with a PivotTable, a SUMIF or a reconciliation.

items.title: Read each question again
items.text: Check the month, the category, the unit and the rounding asked for.

blocks.text: Common slips

items: Not removing duplicate orders, which inflates the count and every total.
Leaving stray spaces or case differences in Region, so a region total comes out short.
Reporting orders when the question asks for units, or revenue when it asks for orders.
Filtering on the category but forgetting the month, or the reverse.
Calculating a share against the wrong total, or rounding too early.
Typing an answer into the wrong place, or with the wrong number of decimals.

blocks.text: Use the sanity checks from the reporting module. Region totals should add up to total revenue. The top region's revenue should be less than the total, and the average order value should sit between the smallest and the largest order. If a number fails one of these tests, go back and look.

blocks.title: Pace yourself
blocks.text: Accuracy matters more than speed. If you are stuck on one question, move on and return to it. Once the data is clean, most of the questions are quick.

blocks.title: Your answers must be your own numbers
blocks.text: The practice file's answers, such as R8,542 and Johannesburg, are for practice only. Your assessment dataset is different. Do not enter practice-file answers, and do not guess. Calculate from the file you downloaded.

blocks.title: A careful check on question 3
blocks.text: A learner finds the top region by revenue using a PivotTable, then cross-checks the same region with a SUMIF. Both give the same figure, and the four region totals add to the overall revenue. Only then does she write the answer down.

blocks.title: Rehearse the practical
blocks.intro: Use the café practice file as if it were the real assessment.
tasks: Set a timer for 60 minutes and answer the eight question types, writing each answer with its units.
Use the checks above and log any number you corrected.
Afterwards, list the three slips you came closest to making.
blocks.reflection: What one habit will you add to your own routine before attempting the practical?

blocks.prompt: Select all that apply. Which of these actions help you avoid errors in the final practical?
options: Keeping an untouched copy of the downloaded file
Cleaning the Region text before calculating by region
Entering the practice file's answers to save time
Checking each answer a second way before writing it down
blocks.explain: A backup, consistent text and a second check all protect your numbers. The practice file's answers belong to different data and would be wrong for your dataset.
